title: Optimizers
subtitle: Module 10 · T1 Chapter 12 · GD variants, momentum, Nesterov, AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam/AdamW, schedules, clipping and tuning

lesson.title: Why optimisation is hard
lesson.lead: No closed form exists for deep networks, so we iterate, and the landscape fights back.

blocks.text: θ* = argmin L(θ)        θ ← θ − η∇L(θ)

head: Challenge
Symptom
rows: ∇L = 0 but not a minimum (some directions up, some down); common in high dimensions
Many local minima; the result depends on initialisation
Zig-zag across the steep direction, crawl along the flat one

lesson.title: The toy problem
lesson.lead: All the deck's numericals use the elongated bowl **L = w₁² + 4w₂²**, starting at (4, 2).

blocks.text: w₂ moves 1.6 on the first step but w₁ only 0.8: the steep direction dominates. That motivates **momentum** (smooth the path) and **adaptive** methods (a different rate per parameter).

lesson.title: Momentum and Nesterov
lesson.lead: Momentum keeps a **velocity**: a running sum of past gradients, like a ball rolling downhill.

blocks.text: vₜ = β vₜ₋₁ + gₜ          θₜ₊₁ = θₜ − η vₜ       (β ≈ 0.9: keep 90% of the old velocity)
Still oscillates in w₂ (2 → 1.2 → 0 → −1.08 → −1.62). Momentum **amplifies** steps, so it needs a smaller η than plain GD.

blocks.label: Convention
blocks.text: Some sources write v = βv + (1 − β)g (an average) or v = βv + ηg. This deck uses **v = βv + g, θ ← θ − ηv**. Say which you use; the answers differ by a constant factor.
Nesterov: vₜ = β vₜ₋₁ + ∇L(θₜ − β vₜ₋₁),  θₜ₊₁ = θₜ − η vₜ
blocks.caption: look ahead first, then compute the gradient: more responsive, slightly faster

lesson.title: AdaGrad and RMSprop
lesson.lead: Adaptive methods divide each parameter's step by the size of its **gradient history**.

blocks.text: AdaGrad:  sₜ = sₜ₋₁ + gₜ²,   θ ← θ − η gₜ / √(sₜ + ε)
blocks.caption: s only grows, so the effective rate shrinks towards 0 and learning stops; good for sparse features

blocks.text: RMSprop:  sₜ = γ sₜ₋₁ + (1 − γ) gₜ²,   θ ← θ − η gₜ / √(sₜ + ε)
blocks.caption: an exponential moving average, so the rate doesn't vanish; γ = 0.9, η = 0.001

blocks.text: The larger gradient (w₂) gets a larger s and so a **smaller** effective rate: both coordinates move about 0.16 per step. Loss 32 → 28.3 → 25.9 → 24.0: steady but slow, with no velocity.

lesson.title: Adam and AdamW
lesson.lead: Adam = **momentum (first moment) + RMSprop (second moment) + bias correction**.

blocks.text: m = β₁m + (1 − β₁)g      v = β₂v + (1 − β₂)g²      m̂ = m/(1 − β₁ᵗ)      v̂ = v/(1 − β₂ᵗ)      θ ← θ − η m̂/(√v̂ + ε)
blocks.caption: defaults β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, η = 0.001, ε = 1e-8

blocks.text: First step on the toy problem (η = 0.05): m = (0.8, 1.6), v = (0.064, 0.256); m̂ = (8, 16), v̂ = (64, 256); step = 0.05 × 8/8 = 0.05 for both → **(3.95, 1.95)**. Early steps are ≈ η per parameter, because m̂/√v̂ ≈ ±1.
Why bias correction? m and v start at 0, so early estimates are biased towards 0. Dividing by (1 − βᵗ) fixes that (at t = 1: m̂ = g, v̂ = g²).
AdamW:  θ ← θ − η ( m̂/(√v̂ + ε) + λθ )
blocks.caption: weight decay applied directly, decoupled from the adaptive scaling; λ = 0.01; usually generalises better than Adam + L2

blocks.label: Comparison from the deck
blocks.text: After 3 steps on the toy (η = 0.05 for all but GD's 0.1): GD 4.21, momentum 8.43, RMSprop 23.9, Adam 28.5. Short-run speed on one toy isn't the whole story: Adam is the robust default.

lesson.title: Learning-rate schedules
lesson.lead: Start large to explore, **decay** to fine-tune; **warm up** big models first.

head: Schedule
Formula
Example
rows: ηₜ = η₀ · t / T_w for t ≤ T_w
η₀ = 0.1, T_w = 5: epoch 2 → 0.04, epoch 5 → 0.1, then decay

blocks.label: Slide check
blocks.text: The slide says the cosine schedule gives 0.001 at epoch 50. With T = 100, cos(π·50/100) = cos(π/2) = 0, so η₅₀ = 0.001 + 0.0495 = **0.0505**. The value 0.001 is reached at epoch 100.

lesson.title: Clipping, batch size and stopping
lesson.lead: Clip exploding gradients, scale η with the batch, and stop early.

blocks.text: norm clipping: g ← g · τ/‖g‖ if ‖g‖ > τ   (τ ≈ 1–5; keeps the direction)        value clipping: gᵢ ← clip(gᵢ, −τ, τ)  (may change direction)
Example: g = (3, 4), ‖g‖ = 5, τ = 1 → g = (0.6, 0.8). Essential for RNNs, Transformers and very deep nets.
**Linear scaling rule:** double the batch → double η (e.g. B 32 at η 0.01 → B 256 at η 0.08), with warmup.

lesson.title: Choosing an optimizer
lesson.lead: **Adam/AdamW** is the default; **SGD + momentum** with careful tuning often generalises best in vision.

head: Optimizer
Key hyperparameters
Best for
rows: Production computer vision, best final accuracy with tuning

items: Watch train/val loss and gradient norms.
Add cosine annealing; warm up big models and batches.

blocks.label: Teacher's tip
blocks.text: Tuning priority: **learning rate first** (try 1e-5 … 1e-2), then batch size, then the schedule; keep optimizer defaults. Common pitfall: η = 0.01 for Adam instead of 0.001.

worked.title: Momentum velocity (EC-3 2026 Q6)

problem.text: β = 0.95, v₀ = 0, gradients 12, 11, 10. Find v after iteration 3. Why can it overshoot? Give two hyperparameter fixes.

steps.label: EMA form
steps.text: If the course uses v = βv + (1 − β)g: 0.6 → 1.12 → **1.564**. State your convention.

steps.label: Overshoot
steps.text: Velocity keeps the push even after the gradient shrinks or flips sign; with β = 0.95 the effective step is ≈ 1/(1 − β) = 20× the gradient, so it runs past the minimum and oscillates.

steps.label: Fixes
steps.text: Lower β (e.g. 0.9 → effective 10×) and/or lower η; add LR decay or warmup; Nesterov momentum looks ahead and brakes earlier.

worked.answer: v₃ = 31.28 (deck form). Reduce β and η.

worked.answer: (3.6, 1.2), (3.84, 1.84), (3.95, 1.95). Adaptive methods equalise the step across directions.

labs.title: Optimizer race
labs.intro: Every optimizer starts from the same point on L = a·w₁² + b·w₂². Pick one for the step table; all paths are drawn together.
tryThis: Momentum with η = 0.05: reproduce the deck's table, including the w₂ oscillation.
Raise b to 20 (a narrower ravine): which optimizer copes best?
Adam with 50 steps: watch it settle; then try η = 0.5.
GD with η = 0.26 and b = 4: it diverges, because η > 2/(2b) = 0.25.

flashcards.front: Why does momentum need a smaller η?
flashcards.back: It accumulates steps (≈ 1/(1 − β) times larger).
Gradient at the look-ahead point θ − βv.
s += g²; θ −= ηg/√(s + ε). Its rate decays to 0.
An exponential moving average of g² instead of a sum.
m = β₁m + (1 − β₁)g, v = β₂v + (1 − β₂)g²
m, v start at 0; dividing by 1 − βᵗ removes the early bias.
AdamW applies weight decay directly (decoupled), not through the gradient.
Large initial steps destabilise big models and batches.
Norm keeps the direction; value clips each component.
Double the batch size → double the learning rate (with warmup).

formulas.name: Momentum (deck)
formulas.formula: v = βv + g;  θ ← θ − ηv

formulas.name: Nesterov
formulas.formula: v = βv + ∇L(θ − βv);  θ ← θ − ηv

formulas.name: AdaGrad
formulas.formula: s += g²;  θ ← θ − ηg/√(s + ε)

formulas.name: RMSprop
formulas.formula: s = γs + (1 − γ)g²;  θ ← θ − ηg/√(s + ε)

formulas.name: Adam
formulas.formula: m = β₁m + (1−β₁)g; v = β₂v + (1−β₂)g²; m̂ = m/(1−β₁ᵗ); v̂ = v/(1−β₂ᵗ); θ ← θ − ηm̂/(√v̂ + ε)
